supplementary_news.content: skip to main content The Magazine STORIES THAT MATTER LoginRegister Stay Curious Search Subscribe The Sciences Mind Technology Health Environment Planet Earth STORIES THAT MATTER Subscribe Health AI Reveals Why Some People Respond Better to the COVID-19 Vaccine Than Others Learn how your antibody fingerprint could reveal whether a vaccine will be effective or not, before you get the shot. Written byStephanie Edwards Stephanie Edwards Stephanie Edwards is the Engagement Specialist at Discover Magazine, who manages all social media platforms and writes digital articles that focus on archaeology, the environment, and public health. View Full Profile. Learn about our Editorial Policy. Aug 20, 2026, 8:49 PM | 3 min read (Image Credit: PeopleImages/Shutterstock) Newsletter Sign up for our email newsletter for the latest science news Sign Up Long before a needle touches the skin, your immune system may have already decided how it's going to respond. Hidden among the antibodies circulating in a person’s blood could be signs of whether an upcoming vaccine will trigger a powerful defense or a comparatively weak response. Vaccines protect most people from severe disease, but their effectiveness is not identical in everyone. A new study published in Cell Press Blue suggests researchers may be able to anticipate some of that variation using pre-vaccination blood samples and artificial intelligence. The findings could eventually help doctors identify people who may benefit from extra doses, closer monitoring, or other protective measures. “What our study found is that certain biomarkers, when analyzed with AI, can predict who is likely to respond well to a vaccine, even before they receive it. This suggests that some people may be more immune-ready than others,” said study lead Joshua LaBaer in a press release. Preexisting Antibodies May Predict Vaccine Response Researchers examined blood samples from more than 4,000 people, measuring antibodies that reacted to 185 antigens. These immune targets included components of familiar viruses and bacteria, along with markers connected to autoimmune diseases. The team compared antibody patterns recorded before and after COVID-19 vaccination. They discovered that elevated levels of several preexisting antibodies were associated with stronger responses to the vaccine, including common microbes like Staphylococcus aureus, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and human respirovirus 3. The scientists suggest these are “sentinel” antibodies because they are not necessarily helping the body attack the vaccine’s intended target. Instead, they may serve as signals of how prepared the antibody-producing portion of the immune system is to spring into action. Read More: COVID-19 Is Spreading Again as a Summer Wave Grows Across the U.S. Why Vaccine Protection Varies Between People Scientists typically assess vaccine response after a vaccine, measuring the antibodies generated against a particular target. This study reversed the question by asking whether someone’s existing immune landscape could forecast their reaction before vaccination. Age, biological sex, genetics, previous infections, and underlying medical conditions can all influence vaccine responses. Immunosuppressive medications or illnesses can also limit the immune system’s ability to react. Yet broad health categories do not tell the entire story. Several immunosuppressed groups in the study were most likely to produce weaker responses, but some immunosuppressed participants still responded strongly. Meanwhile, approximately 5 to 6 percent of otherwise healthy participants had weak responses. That inconsistency suggests immune readiness cannot always be determined from a person’s diagnosis or general health status alone. How AI Could Help Personalize Future Vaccines Rather than relying on one antibody, the researchers trained a deep-learning model to examine patterns across the entire panel. By combining numerous measurements into a larger immune fingerprint, the system could distinguish stronger vaccine responders from weaker ones. This is where AI offers a particular advantage. Biological datasets can contain millions of overlapping data points, making meaningful connections difficult for humans to spot. Machine-learning models can search that complexity for subtle combinations that carry predictive value. The results suggest researchers may learn more by viewing immunity as a landscape shaped by many past encounters with microbes, rather than checking for antibodies against only one pathogen. Although the study focused on COVID-19 vaccination, the method could have wider applications. With further validation, sentinel antibody profiles might support vaccine development and help clinicians recognize patients who need additional doses, follow-up testing, or alternative protection. The future of vaccination may therefore involve more than choosing the right shot — it may also mean understanding the immune system receiving it. This article is not offering medical advice and should be used for informational purposes only. Assam Fresh Covid-19 cases rise in Assam since June; experts rule out severe threat Patients infected with the RF.5 Covid-19 variant are largely showing flu-like symptoms, with no evidence so far of severe illness By Staff Correspondent - 22 Aug 2026 5:54 AM X Representational image (Photo: PTI) The Assam Tribune is now on Whatsapp. Click here to join our channel and stay updated with the latest headlines. Guwahati, Aug 22: Fresh cases of Covid-19 have been reported in Assam over the past two months, but health experts say the infections detected so far have not been severe. Officials said that around 80-90 positive cases were reported in upper Assam during July and August. Also Read - Assam-Meghalaya row: Different resolution timelines emerge after Aug-23 talks The Covid-19 variant circulating in India since June 2026 belongs to the RF.5 subvariant of Omicron, which emerged from the JN.1 lineage. “Patients are showing flu-like or influenza-like symptoms. There is no evidence so far to suggest that RF.5 is causing severe infections,” a microbiologist said. Also Read - Tezpur University VC row: 7 months on, Centre yet to decide on inquiry report Covid-19 cases were also reported in Assam in 2025, with the last cases recorded in December. “However, the latest increase in cases has been observed since the end of June 2026. Sequencing of the variant in the State has not yet been carried out. At present, three viruses are in circulation – Influenza A, Influenza B and Covid-19,” health officials said. Also Read - Nagaland group challenges Assam eviction drive in Golaghat, claims disputed land Officials said that Covid-19 has now become a recurring viral illness, with new variants likely to cause periodic waves of infection. During the recent resurgence of Covid-19 in Andhra Pradesh, health authorities observed that those who succumbed to the infection had underlying chronic conditions, including diabetes and hypertension. Senior citizens, pregnant women and people with underlying health conditions such as diabetes, hypertension and kidney disease continue to remain at greater risk of complications. Also Read - Meghalaya taxi strike continues, Assam vehicles turned back at Umiam, Byrnihat Experts, however, have urged people not to panic, pointing out that the recent rise in cases has been largely limited to localised clusters. They also noted that a large section of the Indian population has developed strong hybrid immunity through previous infections and extensive vaccination. supplementary_news.content: 24/7 LiveRaleighDurhamFayettevilleSurrounding Area 87° COVID 19 COVID-19 activity rising as students head back to school, experts say ByBianca Holman Wednesday, August 19, 2026 4:53PM As summer ends, COVID-19 activity is increasing across the United States, according to health officials. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimate that COVID-19 transmission is rising nationwide. While overall activity levels remain low, infectious disease experts say the virus is spreading more quickly in some regions, particularly in the South. Doctors say seasonal patterns and human behavior often contribute to increases in COVID-19 cases. One spike typically occurs as families return from summer travel and students head back to school. Another increase is commonly seen during the winter months when people spend more time indoors. COVID-19 spreads primarily from person to person through respiratory droplets and aerosols. Common symptoms include cough, sore throat, congestion, fatigue, fever, chills and headaches. Health experts also continue to monitor long COVID, a condition involving lingering symptoms that can persist for weeks or months after an initial infection. Dr. David Wohl, an infectious disease specialist with UNC Health, said new treatment options are available for people who have been exposed to the virus but have not yet developed symptoms. "Let's say someone in your household, your child or somebody else gets COVID-19," Wohl said. "There's now a medicine that was approved at the end of May that you can take that can help prevent infection after exposure. You've been exposed, you're not sick yet, but you're worried and you don't want to get sick." Top Stories Drier air arrives, humidity drops today Back-to-school 2026: What families in Wake, Durham, Cumberland and Orange counties need to know 38 minutes ago 6 arrested after illegal nightclub busted in Durham, ALE says Wohl said the medication is designed to help prevent infection in people who have recently been exposed to the virus. He added that Paxlovid remains available for people who develop COVID-19 and qualify for treatment. Doctors recommend that people who become sick with COVID-19 stay home and limit contact with others until their symptoms improve. An updated COVID-19 vaccine is not yet available, but health care providers expect new doses to arrive in September. Public health officials continue to encourage people to stay informed about local transmission levels, monitor symptoms and seek medical guidance if they believe they have been exposed to the virus. Janette Wong5 Show authors Scientific Reports (2026) Cite this article Save article View saved research 183 Accesses Metrics details We’re sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply. Abstract Social correction has been shown to be effective in reducing misperceptions and limiting the production of harmful content online, but most current evidence comes from platform-run systems or controlled experiments. We evaluate a volunteer-led intervention on Facebook in which trained healthcare workers replied to COVID-19 vaccine-related posts and comments. The intervention used two sources of random variation: randomized ordering of posts on volunteers’ worklists and random assignment of whether drafted replies were posted. We estimate effects on post-level engagement metrics, distinguishing diffusion indicators, measured by shares; interaction indicators, measured by comments; and affective indicators, measured by likes and reactions. The intervention reduced comments on treated posts, with broader declines in some affective responses in randomized-treatment analyses, especially for newer posts and posts classified as anti-vaccine. We find little evidence of reduced sharing. Our results indicate changes in some forms of engagement with treated posts; they do not directly demonstrate reductions in misinformation prevalence, belief change, or exposure patterns. Funding The research described in this paper was funded by Merck Canada, IIS/MISP#: 101560. Author information Authors and Affiliations Ivey Business School, Western University, London, ON, Canada Kirsten Cornelson Michael G. DeGroote School of Medicine, McMaster University, Hamilton, ON, Canada Hao Ming Chen 19 to Zero, Calgary, Canada Caitlin Ford, Jia Hu, Madison Fullerton, Hinna Hasan, Margaret Pateman & Theresa Tang Faculty of Nursing, University of Calgary, Calgary, AB, Canada Margaret Pateman Department of Population Medicine, University of Guelph, Guelph, ON, Canada Janette Wong Authors Kirsten Cornelson View author publications Search author on:PubMed Google Scholar Hao Ming Chen View author publications Search author on:PubMed Google Scholar Caitlin Ford View author publications Search author on:PubMed Google Scholar Jia Hu View author publications Search author on:PubMed Google Scholar Madison Fullerton View author publications Search author on:PubMed Google Scholar Hinna Hasan View author publications Search author on:PubMed Google Scholar Margaret Pateman View author publications Search author on:PubMed Google Scholar Theresa Tang View author publications Search author on:PubMed Google Scholar Janette Wong View author publications Search author on:PubMed Google Scholar Corresponding author Correspondence to Kirsten Cornelson. Ethics declarations Competing interests The authors declare no competing interests. Additional information Publisher’s note Springer Nature remains neutral with regard to jurisdictional claims in published maps and institutional affiliations. Appendices Appendix A: additional intervention details Ethics This project was approved by the University of Calgary Joint Ethics Board (REB22-0315_REN1). The intervention described in the paper was performed in accordance with the guidelines and regulations required by this board. Volunteer recruitment and training Our goal at the beginning of the project was to recruit up to 50 volunteers who were either health care professionals (doctors, nurses, pharmacists, or public health workers) or students in health-related fields. We attempt to recruit using a variety of methods, including (i) advertising on the website of 19 to Zero, our partner organization, (ii) posting on 19 to Zero’s social media accounts, (iii) sending emails to 19 to Zero’s existing volunteer and contact base, and (iv) reaching out to health-related university programs in Canada and asking them to send materials to their students. The advertising material we used offered potential volunteers a chance to combat vaccine hesitancy online and to earn a $300 honorarium and Health Leadership Certificate. Interested individuals were invited to attend online information sessions that were held in mid-2022. Approximately 60 potential volunteers attended the initial information sessions on Zoom, which provided an overview of the goals of the projects and the work that we expected volunteers to do, and provided an opportunity for interested individuals to ask questions to the research team. Following the information session, all participants were contacted by email outlining next steps for a potential engagement. Individuals who indicated an interest in volunteering with us were invited to a further 30 min training session. Prior to attending the session, they were asked to read training materials outlining (i) behavioral principles for combatting vaccine hesitancy, including “good” and “bad” responses to real comments from social media, (ii) tips for how to identify productive conversation opportunities – and which individuals to avoid, and (iii) instructions for how to engage online in a safe way. The training materials are available upon request. During training sessions, volunteers were provided with links to Facebook posts and asked to identify which, if any, comments they would engage with and explain why. They were given feedback on their choices by the research team and other participants. They were then asked to formulate a potential response to comments, and again given feedback. This process was repeated 2–3 times, depending on time constraints. Following training, volunteers were provided with summary documents outlining the process for engagement and the main behavioral principles they should adhere to, as well as links to helpful information on the vaccines. They were also given access to the list of Facebook posts meeting our search criteria. In total, 14 volunteers completed training and went on to participate in the project. Most of these volunteers completed the 30 h we requested in order to be eligible for the honorarium and certificate. Several volunteers signed up for an additional 30 h commitment after this point, and were given an additional honorarium at the end of this commitment. Our volunteers were mostly students, but also included a small number of working health professionals. Process Prior to beginning work with us, volunteers were encouraged to create new Facebook accounts that were not linked to their real Facebook accounts, and that used a version of their names that could not be used to identify them (i.e. “John S.”) and a picture that did not show their faces. They were also encouraged to be honest about the purpose for these accounts by posting information in the biography section indicating that they were health professionals or students, and that they used these accounts to have conversations about the COVID-19 vaccine. When leaving a comment, volunteers were permitted (but not required) to tell people that they were working on behalf of a public health organization. We asked volunteers to friend the Informed Choice Project’s Facebook account with their secondary accounts so that we could keep track of their activity. Volunteers were permitted to work whenever they wanted, although we asked them to put in a minimum of 2 h per week. The process volunteers were asked to follow when completing volunteer hours was: 1) Open key documents, which included: the summary instruction materials we had provided, the sheet with links to vaccine information, and the list of Facebook posts identified by our search. 2) Starting at the top of the list of Facebook posts, open any post that had not yet been worked on by another volunteer (indicated by volunteers putting their names next to the post in the sheet) and read the post and the comments on it. The goal was to identify whether there were any productive engagement opportunities. 3) Once the volunteer decided to leave a comment, they were instructed to open a survey tool in Qualtrics and enter the following information: their name, the link to the post, the name of the individual leaving an original comment (when leaving a reply), and the text of the original comment (when leaving a reply). The tool then randomly instructed them to either leave the comment or not. 4) If they were instructed to leave a comment, they were asked to craft a reply that followed behavioral principles and was based on real information about the vaccine. The information they used to craft this comment could come from our information sources, or they could try to find other information from reputable sources as required. They were then asked to enter the text of their reply into the survey tool, as well as posting it on Facebook. 5) Repeat until they were done a given work session. Once they finished working, they were asked to log their hours using an online volunteer engagement system. The hours were verified by the research team using the information in the Qualtrics database (i.e. we ensured that the volunteer was active in leaving replies during the indicated hours). Data gathering Following the end of the intervention, we downloaded the Qualtrics data containing information about every attempted reply by our volunteers. There were 1,683 attempted replies, of which 174 could not be linked to a URL appearing on our list because of incorrect entry into the “link” field of our form, and 4 appeared to have incorrect dates. The remaining 1,505 attempts were distributed over 736 posts. We used CrowdTangle to get engagement information on every post that ever appeared on our list. We gathered the full engagement history for each of these posts, and then restricted the set of engagement observations to three per post (earliest at least 2 days after creation, latest pre-treatment, latest). We randomly selected a subset of 1,470 non-targeted posts to serve as a control group. Of the 2,206 combined posts, 214 did not have any engagement information available from CrowdTangle (this could occur, for example, if the post was taken down between the time we searched for it and the time when we gathered engagement information). A further 26 were not available as of January 2024, when the research team began the sentiment rating process. A further 34 posts were eliminated because the engagement information provided did not cover both the pre and post treatment period. Finally, 21 posts were eliminated because they were strong outliers on pre-post engagement changes. These restrictions led to a final sample of 2,118 posts, of which 709 had any attempted treatment (273 never treated, 436 treated), and 1,409 did not. Appendix figure 11 below shows the creation of the sample visually, including the number of posts of each type that were lost due to each of the sample restrictions. Measuring vaccine sentiment of posts and comments For parts of the analysis that classify either posts or comments as “pro-vaccine”, “neutral”, or “anti-vaccine”, we relied on researcher ratings of vaccine sentiment. The research team worked from a list of posts presented in random order without any information about treatment. They opened the post and read it, and rated it on a scale from − 10 (very anti-vaccine) to 10 (very pro-vaccine). They then did the same for the first two pre-intervention comments on a post. Two raters attempted to rate each post. Because Meta restricted news to Canadian audiences starting in July 2023, raters could not access all posts from Canada at the time rating started in January 2024. One rater was sent to the United States to complete rating for these posts. Anti-vaccine posts and comments could be either directly related to the vaccine, or related to other types of misinformation relevant to the vaccine (in particular, the effectiveness of masking and the use of ivermectin as a treatment for COVID-19). News headlines, particularly from mainstream news organizations, were typically rated as neutral. Pro-vaccine posts were most commonly announcements from public health organizations encouraging the use of the vaccine–although there were also posts from fact-checking and pro-science organizations included in this group. When rating posts and comments, the researchers took into account sentiment on issues that were highly correlated with attitudes about the vaccine, including: the efficacy of masking, the belief that the COVID-19 pandemic was a government conspiracy, the efficacy of Ivermectin as a treatment for COVID, the belief that COVID-19 was “just a cold”, etc. Posts or comments supporting these positions were rated as anti-vaccine. News stories from major outlets about the vaccine were typically rated as neutral, unless they were written in a way that was clearly pro- or anti-vaccine. Appendix B: Robustness checks Excluding non-compliant volunteers As noted in the main paper, there were two volunteers for whom we could not verify any of the comments they recorded. We are unclear as to whether these volunteers left the comments and deleted them at the end of the intervention, or never left the comments. Appendix figure 12 shows how the results for the main sample change if we exclude posts treated by these volunteers. The results are nearly identical, but slightly stronger if we exclude these posts. Outlier management In the course of analysis, we noticed that there were some strong outliers that saw very strong changes in engagement from the pre-intervention to post-intervention period. Appendix figure 13 shows the raw change in the engagement index from pre- to post-intervention, plotted against randomized rank order. As the figure shows, these observations are mostly untreated and most (but not all) appeared towards the bottom of the volunteers’ list. The latter feature means that they have the potential to create a relationship between engagement and rank or treatment that is not driven by the intervention. In our main results, we eliminate these observations by excluding 21 posts that have changes in the engagement index (residualized after accounting for control variables) that are more than 3 standard deviations away from the mean. Appendix figure 14 shows how the results change when we do not impose this restriction. When outliers are included, the results for randomized rank order become 10–20 times larger and are statistically significant for 4 of the 6 outcomes. The randomized treatment results remain relatively similar to those in the main text, although are slightly smaller and less statistically significant. The size of the rank order results when including outliers suggests that the relationships they document between rank order and engagement are not purely due to rank order affecting treatment. For example, the implied IV effect of treatment on the engagement index in this case is 0.069 SD – about 15 times higher than the effect we estimate using random treatment. Because this result is driven by a small number of observations, we consider it more prudent to exclude these observations. Note that while the relative magnitude of the results is sensitive to the inclusion of outliers, the main conclusion of the paper – that our intervention reduced some forms of engagement – holds in both cases. Sensitivity to different raters: post sentiment As noted in the main text, our two raters had high levels of agreement when it came to the rating the sentiment of the original posts. We unpacked the federal grant and research fueling the conspiracy theory. Megan Loe August 23, 2026 SUNDAY READ Welcome to this special edition of Snopes’ newsletter. Today, we’re investigating a persistent rumor claiming Dr. Fauci funded research that allegedly caused the COVID-19 pandemic. Did Fauci fund Chinese research that caused COVID-19? More than six years after the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, gaps in our knowledge about its origin are still fueling speculation and conspiracy theories. One persistent rumor accuses Dr. Anthony Fauci of funding research at a lab in China that supposedly created a genetically modified virus and caused the pandemic. While the allegations are based on real, NIH-funded research into bat coronaviruses, the narrative draws conclusions that aren’t backed by evidence. In this exclusive report, we unpack: The competing theories behind the pandemic’s origin. The debate over “gain-of-function” research. The federal grant fueling the conspiracy theory involving Fauci. The specific viruses at the center of the Wuhan lab’s research. Follow Former Fauci advisor pleads guilty to conspiring to conceal COVID-19 records Robert McGreevy Wed, August 19, 2026 at 6:01 PM UTC 3 min read Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. David Morens, a former advisor to Dr. Anthony Fauci and senior official at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID), pleaded guilty Tuesday to conspiring to evade records requests involving COVID-19 research grants, FBI Director Kash Patel announced. "After an FBI investigation with our DOJ partners, Dr. Fauci's associate, David Morens, just pleaded guilty to conspiracy in a scheme to avoid FOIA requests and the Federal Records Act connected to COVID-19 research grants," Patel wrote in a Tuesday post on X. "The FBI uncovered that Morens, Co-Conspirator 1, Co-Conspirator 2, and others conspired during the COVID-19 pandemic to defraud the United States after the National Institutes of Health terminated Co-Conspirator 1's grant," Patel's post continued. Advertisement Advertisement "NIH terminated the grant, 'Understanding the Risk of Bat coronavirus Emergence,' based on allegations that COVID-19 emerged from the Wuhan Institute of Virology (WIV) in Wuhan, China. Mr. Morens and his co-conspirators then agreed in writing to intentionally hide their communications from public view by corresponding through Morens's personal Gmail account rather than his official NIH email account," Patel also added. Rand Paul Brings Cia Whistleblower To Senate Hearing Alleging 'Deep State' Covid-19 Conspiracy David Morens leaves the U.S. District Court following his arraignment on felony charges alleging he concealed communications related to virus research from Freedom of Information Act requests, May 8, 2026, in Greenbelt, Maryland. The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) indicted Morens in April, charging him with conspiracy, destruction and concealment of federal records and related offenses. Read On The Fox News App Fauci's Diary Shows He Fed Questions To Journalists, Built Friendships With Media Figures Morens, it was revealed after the House Select Subcommittee on the Coronavirus Pandemic acquired his emails, instructed colleagues to circumvent his official NIAID email and communicate with him through his private email address. Dr. David Morens testifies before the House Select Subcommittee on the Coronavirus Pandemic on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., on May 22, 2024, regarding allegations about deleting emails related to COVID-19. "This is sent from my gmail account. Please send all replies here To gmail... There are things I cant say except [Senior NIAID official 1] is aware and I have learned that there are ongoing efforts within NIH to steer through this with minimal damage to you, [Co-Conspirator 1], and colleagues, and to nih and niaid," Morens wrote to a colleague, according to emails released by the committee. Fauci Held In Contempt As Covid Cellphone Lands In Hands Of senate Investigators In another email Morens wrote to EcoHealth Alliance President Peter Daszak, Morens appeared to recount how a Fauci aide instructed him to delete emails. Dr. Anthony Fauci testifies to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee hearing on July 29, 2026, in Washington, D.C. "I learned from your FOIA lady here now how to make emails disappeared when I am FOIA'ed but before the search starts, so I think we are all safe. Plus, I deleted most of these earlier emails after sending them to Gmail," he wrote in 2021. Advertisement Advertisement "In another email, dated 4/21/21, Morens wrote, "I forgot to say, there is no worry about FOIAs. I can either send stuff to Tony on his private email or hand it to him at work or at his house. He is too smart to let colleagues send him stuff that could cause trouble.'' Daszak, who ran the EcoHealth firm that obtained a federal grant to study coronaviruses in China, was debarred from receiving federal grant funding in 2025 after allegedly failing to disclose the grant's role in funding gain-of-function research on viruses. Advertisement Advertisement "By pleading guilty today, Dr. Morens has taken responsibility for what he did, and he will continue to do so," Morens' attorney Timothy Belevetz said in a statement, according to NBC News. Fox News Digital contacted Morens' attorney, the DOJ and the NIAID for further comment. David Morens, who had worked under Fauci as a senior official at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases during the pandemic, entered his plea to a conspiracy charge during a hearing in federal court in Greenbelt, Maryland. The 78-year-old had been indicted ​in April on charges related to what prosecutors said was a scheme to thwart ​public records requests received by the agency beginning in April 2020 related ⁠to Covid-19 research grants. The jury will soon answer a more complicated question. The FBI said in 2023 that a leak from a Wuhan laboratory likely caused the pandemic, a claim China said had “no credibility whatsoever.” The CIA said in January 2025 a lab leak was likely, but with “low confidence,” while four other U.S. intelligence agencies and the National Intelligence Council believe the virus most likely emerged via natural transmission from some animal. Prosecutors said that Morens’ plea related to the National Institutes of Health’s decision to cancel a research grant related to bat coronavirus, based on allegations that Covid-19 emerged from the Wuhan lab. The China-based lab had received a sub-award from the company that had received the grant. Prosecutors said that Morens pledged to help restore the bat coronavirus grant and counter the narrative Covid-19 leaked from a lab. Anticipating their communications would be sought through Freedom of Information Act requests, Morens and others agreed to correspond using Morens’ personal email account instead of his government one, prosecutors said. Ex-Fauci Adviser Pleads Guilty In COVID-19 Records Scheme Dr. David Morens faces up to five years in prison after admitting to conspiring to conceal documents related to the pandemic and grant research. By Nina Golgowski Senior Breaking News Reporter, HuffPost Aug 19, 2026, 03:46 PM EDT Leave a Comment LOADINGERROR LOADING A former senior adviser to infectious disease expert Dr. Anthony Fauci has pleaded guilty to conspiring to conceal government documents related to the COVID-19 pandemic and grant research funding. Dr. David Morens, 78, pleaded guilty in a Maryland federal court on Tuesday to conspiring to defraud the U.S. government. He faces up to five years in prison and will be sentenced on Nov. 12. Advertisement “By pleading guilty today, Dr. Morens has taken responsibility for what he did, and he will continue to do so,” defense attorney Tim Belevetz said in a statement shared with media outlets. Fauci, who has been demonized by Republicans over his handling of the pandemic, was not charged in the case. Dr. David Morens testified in 2024 about his role as a senior adviser at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases during the COVID-19 pandemic. The Washington Post via Getty Images Advertisement Prosecutors said Morens, while working as a senior adviser with the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, or NIAID, used his personal email account to intentionally conceal or destroy records of discussions related to COVID-19 research grants and an investigation into the pandemic’s origins. Prosecutors said he did this while receiving gifts from the CEO of a New York-based nonprofit who wanted the National Institutes of Health, which NIAID is part of, to revive a 2014 grant for the nonprofit’s research into the emergence of bat coronaviruses. The CEO’s and nonprofit’s names are redacted in the indictment. “[I] learned from our [Freedom of Information Act] lady here how to make emails disappear after I am FOIA’d but before the search starts, so I think we are all safe. Plus I deleted most of those earlier emails after sending them to gmail,” Morens wrote in one email to the nonprofit CEO and to a co-investigator of the grant in early 2021, according to his criminal indictment. Advertisement The nonprofit, identified in a related congressional investigation as the since-defunct EcoHealth Alliance, worked closely with the Wuhan Institute of Virology in China, which, according to one theory popularized by the White House and Republicans, conducted research that may have allowed the coronavirus to spread to humans. Scientists remain divided on the origins of the pandemic, however. Morens, who resigned from the NIAID in 2022, had denied trying to evade federal transparency laws by using his personal email while testifying before a congressional committee about his actions in 2024. That denial came as House Republicans investigated the coronavirus’ origins and EcoHealth’s ties to the Wuhan Institute of Virology. By Marcela Camargo • Published August 22, 2026 • Updated on August 22, 2026 at 3:01 pm Log in or create a free profile to save articles BOOKMARKER Live Unmute Subtitles EnglishNoneSettings ShareToggle Fullscreen Look who it is. A New Jersey real estate investor pleaded guilty earlier this week to participating in a multimillion-dollar mortgage fraud scheme and fraudulently obtaining more than $1.8 million in COVID-19 relief loans, according to U.S. Attorney Robert Frazer. Officials said 39-year-old Arthur Spitzer, of Toms River, pleaded guilty Wednesday to one count of bank and wire fraud conspiracy and one count of money laundering in connection with the fraud schemes. Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10. WATCH HERE According to prosecutors, who cited court documents and statements made in court, in June 2020, Spitzer conspired with Mendel Deutsch and Joshua Feldberger, who are both awaiting sentencing, to make it appear as though Spitzer owned three properties in Brooklyn, New York, and had agreed to sell them to Deutsch, who obtained a $4.5 million mortgage loan in connection with the transaction. Prosecutors said Feldberger facilitated the fraudulent transaction as the owner of the settlement company that handled it. According to officials, the defendants also created and sent letters stating that Deutsch had deposited significant funds into escrow toward the transaction when, in reality, he had not. Instead, they created fake documentation purportedly transferring control of the properties to Spitzer and made false statements to the mortgage lender, claiming that the settlement company had received more than $2 million from Deutsch at closing. Those statements led the mortgage lender to fund the loan. The men then used the mortgage loan proceeds to fund Deutsch’s down payment, which he had supposedly already provided, prosecutors said. According to officials, Spitzer also admitted that he was responsible for the losses resulting from five additional fraudulent loan schemes in 2019 and 2020, totaling more than $10 million. Local Breaking news and the stories that matter to your neighborhood. First Alert Weather 8 hours ago Sunshine returns with calm, dry stretch of weather ahead Philadelphia 8 hours ago 64-year-old killed in Frankford shooting; man taken into custody In 2020 and 2021, Spitzer also fraudulently obtained approximately $1.8 million in government loans intended for small businesses distressed by the COVID-19 pandemic, prosecutors said. The CARES Act authorized the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) to provide Economic Injury Disaster Loans (EIDLs) of up to $2 million to eligible small businesses that were experiencing substantial financial disruption due to the COVID-19 pandemic. To obtain an EIDL loan, a qualifying small business was required to submit an application and provide information on its operations, including the number of employees and revenues or expenses. Prosecutors said Spitzer obtained EIDLs for businesses with little or no operations by submitting loan applications containing false statements about the applicant companies’ number of employees, revenues, cost of goods sold or lost rents. According to officials, Spitzer then laundered some of the proceeds from the EIDL fraud. The bank and wire fraud conspiracy count is punishable by a maximum of 30 years in prison and a $1 million fine, or twice the gross gain or loss from the offense. The money laundering count is punishable by a maximum of 10 years in prison and a $250,000 fine, or twice the gross gain or loss from the offense. Spitzer has agreed to pay full restitution to the victims, including $1 million to the true owner of the Brooklyn properties and at least $1,845,400 to the SBA, subject to any applicable credits for amounts already repaid to the victims. Spitzer also agreed to forfeit $2.25 million in connection with the bank and wire fraud conspiracy and $100,000 in connection with the laundering of fraudulent EIDL proceeds, for a total of $2.35 million. Spitzer is scheduled to be sentenced on Dec. 21, 2026. Deutsch is scheduled to be sentenced on Oct. 6, 2026, and Feldberger is awaiting a new sentencing date. Sisti, CCRP Current Page Resha B. Sisti, CCRP Resha Sisti, CCRP, joined St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital in 2012 and currently is a Clinical Research Associate II in the Department of Bone Marrow Transplantation and Cellular Therapy. When Sisti initially arrived at St. Jude, she joined the Department of Immunology, spending 10 years engaged in immunology-focused research. Her work included projects on T cell responses, TCR diversity, and host responses to infection. During her time in the lab, she gained hands-on experience in virus recovery, generating ferret monoclonal antibodies, flow cytometry, CRISPR Cas9 gene editing, embryonic stem cell targeting and culture etc. Over time, Sisti’s interests began to shift toward clinical research. As her involvement in human studies expanded, she took oversight of multiple human sample projects within the lab, which ultimately led her to formally transition into a clinical research associate role. As the first CRA in the department, Sisti managed regulatory responsibilities for multiple human studies involving samples from collaborating sites. Working under rapidly evolving conditions during Covid19, she collaborated with multiple teams to help develop protocol, consents, establish SOPs for sample processing and distribution, and manage extensive blood sample processing efforts for SJTRC study involving SJ employees. As her experience in clinical research grew, the Kathmandu, Nepal, native sought greater exposure to patient-centered research and joined the Bone Marrow Transplantation and Cellular Therapy team. Working alongside a highly dedicated clinical research team, she has taken the lead on multiple protocols and gained experience in developing studies from the ground up. In BMTCT, she is a part of the hematologic malignancy team and has been involved with the Transplant, Virus Specific T cell and CAR-T protocols. Collaborating across departments has reinforced her understanding that successful clinical research is a collective effort, with each team contributing unique expertise toward improving patient outcomes. Pursuing a master's degree in the St. Jude Graduate Schools’ Clinical Investigations program represents an opportunity to deepen her understanding of clinical research from a broader and more structured perspective. Sisti aims to apply the skills gained through this program to advance her career, take on mentorship and leadership roles, and contribute to the development and execution of impactful clinical protocols. Sisti believes the program will provide the knowledge, skills, and confidence necessary to help her achieve these goals and continue growing as a clinical research professional.
